say: Welcome, Shape Detectives! Today we fold things: paper into cubes, and pictures in half in our heads.
Some shapes made of 6 squares fold into a perfect cube and some do not. By the end you will be able to tell which, without cutting. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
I will show a letter made of squares. Imagine folding it so the two halves match exactly. How many different ways can you fold it? Show me with your fingers.
Then tell me where the fold line goes: up and down, or across?
You have 6 squares. Do you think EVERY shape you make with them will fold into a cube? Write yes or no in the corner of your whiteboard.
stuck: Stuck: start with 4 squares in a row, which wrap round to make the walls. Where can the other two go?
Not sure if it is new: "Is it the same as one we have, just turned or flipped over?"
Finished early: find a shape that does NOT fold. Why does it fail?

say: “I choose a base: a square with lots of neighbours. The squares touching it fold up and become walls: left, right and back. This square is joined to the right wall, so when the right wall stands up it swings round to the front. The last square folds over the top: the lid. One base, four walls, one lid. It works.”

“This one: base in the middle. Two walls go up, front and back. This square hangs from the back wall and swings round to the left. But this other one hangs from the front wall and ALSO swings to the left. Two squares in the same place, and nothing on the right. Not a net.”

“Opposite faces: in a straight line of 3, the two ends are opposite, because the middle one folds between them. At the two ends of a step, the ends are opposite too. Then the last two letters must be the last pair.”

do: Ask: “Which square is your base? Which ones become walls?”
Ask: “Which face lands on top of this one? Is anything already there?”
Ask: “How many squares is this corner from the line? Where is its partner?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Shade the base. Fold the walls up one at a time with your finger.”
Hint 2: “Look for a straight line of 3 squares. The ends are opposite.”
Hint 3: “Count the squares from the dashed line to each corner. Put a dot the same number of squares on the other side.”

say: “Mei says every shape made of 6 squares folds into a cube. Ben says a shape with 4 squares in a row always does. Who is right?”
ask: “Mei says every shape made of 6 squares folds into a cube. Ben says a shape with 4 squares in a row always does. Who is right?”

Neither is right. A 2 by 3 rectangle has 6 squares but does not fold into a cube (Mei is wrong). A row of 4 with both extra squares on the same side does not fold either, because both close the same end (Ben is wrong).

say: “You folded cubes in your head today, and you found the hidden partners in symmetric shapes.”
“Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p4l8-title.note: Objective: Decide whether a shape made of 6 squares folds into a cube by folding it in your head, find which faces of a net are opposite (and use it for dice), complete a figure so that a given line is a line of symmetry, find all the lines of symmetry of a shape, and shade squares to make a pattern symmetric. Thinking strategies taught today: FOLD IT IN YOUR HEAD (base, walls, lid), TEST EVERY CASE, and COUNT THE SQUARES FROM THE LINE. Materials: squared paper (2 cm squares), scissors, sticky tape, 6 paper squares per child, a dice, a small mirror (optional), mini whiteboards, coloured pencils. Online: children cut out 6 paper squares before the lesson and fold on camera; the tutor clicks to reveal each fold on the slides and shades the grids. Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 2.5-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6.5 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 8.5 to 11.5 (three questions). Explore 11.5 to 25.5 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 25.5 to 34 (click to reveal each step and answer; the one "your turn" slide is optional: skip it if you are behind). Brain break 34 to 37.5 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 37.5 to 80: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 37.5 to 56.5, check together 56.5 to 59, short teaching before page 2 59 to 62.5, page 2 on your own 62.5 to 77.5 (the last 2.5 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 77.5 to 80. Talk time 80 to 85 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout; one minute is the tool question: where did you use today's tool?). Exit ticket 85 to 87.5. Looking back 87.5 to 90 (common look-back: 90-second timer, then about 60 seconds to stamp journals). After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children). SPINE: Today's tool is Act it out. Use objects, folding or a role-play to see what happens, then record it. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p4l8-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6.5 (5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) 2 fold lines: one up-down line through the middle and one across the middle. (Plain block H.) 2) No. The first 4 squares wrap round as walls. The 5th lands on top of the 1st and the 6th on top of the 2nd, so nothing makes a lid or a base. A GOOD REASON: A net needs one base, one lid and four walls with nothing overlapping. A line of symmetry is a fold where both halves match exactly. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l8-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Fold It in Your Head. Show one letter at a time (the clicks reveal H, T, E, L, U, Z in order). Count 3, 2, 1: fingers up for the number of lines of symmetry. Then a child shows with a finger where the fold line goes. Answers: H 2 (up-down and across), T 1 (up-down), E 1 (across), L 0, U 1 (up-down), Z 0. A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves match exactly. Z is the surprise: it looks balanced, but folding it never makes the halves match (it turns upside down onto itself, which is a different idea). Hold up a small mirror along a line if you have one: if the picture in the mirror looks like the whole letter, it is a line of symmetry.

p4l8-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 11.5. Hold up a real cube or dice if you can. Three questions, about 30 seconds each: write it, say the answer together on three, then click. No follow-up questions. Answers: 6, 12, 8. The other two warm-up questions (what is opposite 3 on a dice; how many folds of a rectangle make the halves match) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l8-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 22. Pairs join 6 paper squares and try to fold them into a cube. Families cut the six squares (from the Square grid cut-out page) BEFORE the lesson, so these minutes are joining, folding and drawing, not cutting (online: fold on camera, or draw the shape on squared paper and fold in their heads). Ask them to predict first: "Will every shape work?" Let them find out. Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: find a shape that does NOT fold into a cube, and say why it fails. GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): What if the longest row has only 3 squares? Can the shape still fold into a cube? Find one. Answer: Yes. 4 of the 11 cube nets have a longest row of 3 squares. One example: two rows of 3 squares, where the second row starts under the last square of the first row. (One net, the staircase, has no row longer than 2.)

p4l8-explore2.note: Minutes 22 to 25.5. Pencils down (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms), then gather the shapes on the board. Two debrief questions only. Ask "Is this one the same as that one, just turned or flipped?" Answers: 1) There are 11 different nets of a cube altogether (turned or flipped copies count as the same); most groups find 4 to 7. 2) Two squares landed on the same face: for example a 2 by 2 block (4 squares meeting at a corner, but only 3 faces meet at a cube corner), 5 squares in a row, or two squares closing the same end. The third question (do all the shapes that work have 4 squares in a row? No: the staircase and the 3-3 net have a row of 3 and no row of 4) is not asked. Do NOT give the method yet if nobody finds it; the teaching part comes next.

p4l8-teach1.note: Use 6 paper squares, tape and a real cube if possible. Ask first: "Do you think this folds into a cube?" Take guesses. Click 1: the base (yellow). Click 2: fold the left, right and back squares up with your finger: they stand like walls. Click 3: "This square hangs from the RIGHT wall, so when the wall stands up it swings round to the front." Click 4: the lid. Think-aloud: "A cube has 6 faces: one base, one lid and four walls. I check I have all four walls: left, right, back, front, and nothing is in the same place twice." Then fold the paper model to prove it.

p4l8-we1.note: Click 1: base and the two walls beside it. Click 2: "The end square is the lid. The square above the left wall: when that wall stands up, the square swings round to the back." Click 3: "Now the square above the end square. The lid has folded over the top, so this square swings to the back too." Ask: "How many squares are at the back? How many at the front?" (2 and 0.) Think-aloud: "A net needs one of each face. Here the back is covered twice and the front is empty. It fails." Say: Having 4 squares in a row does NOT guarantee a net: where the other two squares go matters. (They must be on different sides, or both on the inside of the row.)

p4l8-we2.note: Teach before the worksheet (Q2 has a different net). Use the paper model: lay it flat, fold it, and point to the faces. Click 1: "Look along the row: B, C, D. When I fold, C is the bottom and B and D stand up on opposite sides. So B and D face each other." Click 2: the same going down: A, B, F. Click 3: C, D, E. Do NOT say "squares next to each other are opposite": opposite faces have exactly ONE square between them in a line. Ask: "Which net squares are NOT in a line of 3? Can you still find their partner?" (The last pair is what is left over.)

p4l8-try2.note: Whiteboards, then click. The ends of the vertical line of 3 (6, 3, ?) are opposite, so the square below the 3 is 1 (6 + 1 = 7). The horizontal row is 2, 3, ?, ?: the 2 and the square two to its right are opposite, so that is 5 (2 + 5 = 7). The last square is the end of the row, opposite the 3: 4 (3 + 4 = 7). Check: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 all appear once.

p4l8-key.note: Say the key ideas together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Thinking any 6 squares make a cube, and ticking shapes with a 2 by 2 block, 5 squares in a row, or two squares that close the same end. (2) Saying two squares next to each other are opposite, instead of the ends of a line of 3. (3) Saying a rectangle has 4 lines of symmetry (the diagonal does not work), or completing a symmetric figure by sliding the half across instead of flipping it.

p4l8-break.note: 3.5 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 37.5): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. Online: the tutor is the leader and all the children are mirrors. The mirror uses the right hand when the leader raises the left. Then swap. This is the idea behind a line of symmetry: the mirror image.

p4l8-ws1.note: Minutes 37.5 to 56.5. Pairs do Q1 to Q3. A child who is slow on Q1 (mental folding) still has Q2 and Q3 as the carry-on questions. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. For Q1 ask pairs to fold each shape in their heads first, then check one with paper. For Q3(b) ask: "Which squares are the ends of a line of 3?" CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l8-ws1ans.note: Click after a pair explains. Q1: A is the cross (4 in a row with one above and one below the second square); C is the 3-3 net; E is the staircase; B puts both squares on the same side at the ends so they cover the same face; D has 5 in a row, so the 5th lands on the 1st; F has a 2 by 2 block. Q2: the net is a staircase. B, C, D is a line of 3, so B and D are opposite. A is above B and E is below D: they are the two ends of the step, so A and E are opposite. The last pair is C and F. Q3a: 1 is opposite 6; the row reads 3, 5, 4, 2 and the last square is 6. Q3b: 5 is opposite 2, 1 is opposite 6, 3 is opposite 4.

p4l8-teachsym.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 has a rocket and a fish; this is a house). Click 1: run a finger along the row of squares from the line to the roof corner: 4. "A partner is the same distance on the other side." Click 2: the bottom corner. Click 3: join. Think-aloud: "Every corner needs a partner at the same height and the same distance from the line. I count squares; I do not guess." Common mistake: copying the half by sliding it to the right (it would look the same but not flipped). Ask: "If the left roof slopes down to the left, which way does the right roof slope?"

p4l8-teachlines.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Use a paper rectangle: fold it up-down and across (the halves match) and then fold it corner to corner (the corners do not meet: the long edge lies beside the short edge). Systematic method: try up-down, across, then the two corner-to-corner lines, and mark each that works. Mention: a shape can have 0 lines (like the letter Z); that is a perfectly good answer.

p4l8-teachshade.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6 has a different pattern and two lines). Method: take each shaded square in turn, flip it over the line, and check the partner is shaded. A square with an unshaded partner is the clue: that partner is the one to shade. Ask: "Could I shade a different square instead?" (No: any other square would have no partner.) Q6 on the worksheet has two dashed lines, so there are two ways: one for each line.

p4l8-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who count the diagonal of a rectangle as a line of symmetry. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q4 and Q5 first. Q6 is a choice for the last few minutes. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 2.5 minutes of this block (minute 75 to 77.5) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l8-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q4: ask a child to say "this corner is 2 squares from the line, so its partner is 2 squares on the other side". Q5: the H has up-down and across; the plus has up-down, across and two corner-to-corner lines; the zigzag of 4 (an S shape) has none: it can be turned half a turn onto itself but never folded. Q6: shade A2: B2 has partner C2 across the up-down line; D2 needs A2. Shade D3: the across line needs B2 with B3, C2 with C3, and D2 with D3 (B3 and C3 are already shaded).

p4l8-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) 22 squares: 2 faces of 3 by 2 (6 each), 2 faces of 3 by 1 (3 each) and 2 faces of 2 by 1 (2 each). 12 + 6 + 4 = 22. 2) Bottom 4 (3 + 4 = 7). Back 2 (5 + 2 = 7). 3) 2. All six faces add up to 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21, and 21 − 19 = 2. 4) Only the T. The line has 2, the square has 4, the L and the zigzag have 0.

p4l8-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) 3 (two dice have 42 altogether; the 2 hidden faces are equal and 42 − 36 = 6, so each is 3). 2) The centre and the 4 corners (an X), or the centre and the 4 edge-middle squares (a plus).

p4l8-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: Q1 "How many faces does one dice have? How many faces are hidden in all?" Q2 "Which square lies on ALL four lines? Which squares are partners under every line?" Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l8-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the trick is to count the hidden faces, not the visible ones. Check: if the glued number were 2, the hidden total would be 4 and the visible total 38. Q2: a square on a line of symmetry stays put when we fold along that line; the middle square lies on all four, so it must be shaded for any pattern to be symmetric under every line (or be empty). A corner square flips to another corner, so if one corner is shaded all four must be: that is a team of 4. The edge-middle squares are another team of 4.

p4l8-talk.note: Minutes 80 to 85. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then share. Answer: neither is right. A 2 by 3 rectangle has 6 squares and does not fold (it has a 2 by 2 block), so Mei is wrong. A row of 4 with one square above each end does not fold either, because both extra squares cover the back, so Ben is wrong. One counter-example is enough to show a rule is not always true. Not asked in class (moved to the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math): "How can you tell two faces are opposite without folding?" (They are the ends of a line of 3 squares.) Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake. TOOL MINUTE: Talk time is one minute longer than before (the common look-back is shorter). Spend it on the question on the slide: where did you use today's tool, and what did it help you see? Listen for the tool named, not for the answer; a child may pass.

p4l8-exit.note: Minutes 85 to 87.5. Answer: 4. The 3, 2, 1 and ? squares make a staircase: the 3 and the ? are the two ends of the step, so they are opposite, and 3 + 4 = 7. Children who write 6 or 5 chose a square next to it. Extension: fill in the other two squares. The square right of the ? is opposite the 1, so 6; the bottom-right square is opposite the 2, so 5.

p4l8-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 87.5 to 90. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals.
